title: Healthy Eating During Pregnancy: A Guide to the Foods for You and Your Baby
metaTitle: Healthy Eating During Pregnancy: Foods, Nutrients & Safety
metaDescription: Learn about healthy eating during pregnancy, essential nutrients, nutritious food choices, hydration, food safety, and foods to limit or avoid.
excerpt: A patient-friendly guide to nutrients, balanced food choices, hydration, food safety, and dietary considerations during pregnancy.
author: Dr. Farkhanda Kashif

featuredImage.alt: Abstract illustration of leaves and a bowl representing pregnancy nutrition education

body.text: Pregnancy is an exciting time filled with many changes, and one of the most important ways to support a healthy pregnancy is through good nutrition. Every meal provides an opportunity to nourish both your body and your growing baby. While no single “superfood” can guarantee a healthy pregnancy, eating a balanced diet rich in essential nutrients helps support your baby’s development, reduces the risk of certain pregnancy complications, and promotes your overall wellbeing.
Why healthy eating matters during pregnancy
Your nutritional needs increase during pregnancy because your body is supporting:

items: Growth of the fetus and placenta
Development of your baby’s brain, bones, muscles, and organs

body.text: A nutritious, balanced diet can also help lower the risk of:

items: Gestational diabetes when combined with healthy lifestyle habits

body.title: Focus on eating better, not simply more
body.text: Rather than “eating for two,” focus on eating better, not simply more. Most pregnant women only need modest increases in calorie intake during pregnancy.
Essential nutrients during pregnancy
Folate (folic acid)
Folate is one of the most important nutrients during early pregnancy because it helps prevent neural tube defects affecting the baby’s brain and spinal cord.
Good food sources include:

items: Dark green leafy vegetables and spinach

body.title: Folic acid supplements
body.text: Even with a healthy diet, healthcare providers recommend taking folic acid supplements before conception and during early pregnancy.
Protein
Protein supports your health and your baby’s growth and helps build muscles, organs, skin, and the placenta.

Calcium supports healthy development of bones, teeth, the heart, nerves, and muscles.

Omega-3 fatty acids
Omega-3 fats, particularly DHA, are important for brain development and nervous system development.
Healthy sources include:

body.title: Choose fish low in mercury
body.text: Choose fish that are low in mercury and avoid high-mercury species such as shark, swordfish, king mackerel, and marlin.
Fibre
Pregnancy hormones slow digestion, making constipation common. Fibre helps improve bowel movements, promote healthy digestion, reduce constipation, and support healthy blood sugar control.
High-fibre foods include:
Drink plenty of water to help fibre work effectively.
Vitamin D
Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium and supports healthy bones and immune function.
Sources include:
Many pregnant women may require vitamin D supplementation because food sources alone may not provide enough.
Iodine
Iodine requirements rise markedly during pregnancy and lactation. Adequate intake is essential because iodine supports healthy fetal brain and neurocognitive development.

Most women of reproductive age typically consume enough iodine, but those who rarely eat dairy products, eggs, seafood, or who do not use iodized salt may fall short of the increased demands during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Pregnant women should make sure that any salt used in cooking or at the table is iodized.
Because iodine needs rise during pregnancy and breastfeeding, some women may also require an iodine-containing supplement to meet recommended intake.
Choline

Choline needs rise significantly during pregnancy and lactation. Getting enough choline during these stages helps restore maternal stores and supports healthy development of the baby’s brain and spinal cord.

Many women do not meet the recommended choline intake during pregnancy. Choline is found across several food groups, with notable sources including eggs, dairy, meats, safe seafood, beans, peas, and lentils.

Food should ideally provide the needed choline, but women who are unsure about meeting recommendations should speak with their healthcare provider to determine whether choline supplementation is appropriate.
Healthy foods to eat during pregnancy
Fruits
Fresh fruits provide vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, and fibre. Excellent choices include:

items: Pears, mangoes, kiwi, grapes, and pomegranates

body.text: Aim for a variety of colourful fruits throughout the week.
Vegetables
Vegetables are rich in vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. Try to include:

items: Sweet potatoes, bell peppers, and tomatoes

body.text: A colourful vegetable plate often provides a wider range of nutrients.
Whole grains

Whole grains provide energy, fibre, and vitamins. Options include oatmeal, brown rice, whole wheat bread, whole wheat pasta, and whole grain cereals. Whole grains help maintain steady energy levels throughout the day.
Dairy foods
Dairy products are rich in calcium, iodine, and protein. Healthy options include:

items: Cheese made from pasteurized milk and cottage cheese

body.text: Choose lower-fat options if recommended by your healthcare provider.
Healthy fats
Healthy fats give you energy and support fetal development. Good choices include avocados, olive oil, nuts, and seeds. These foods also help you feel satisfied after meals.
Healthy snacks during pregnancy
Nutritious snacks can help maintain energy between meals. Examples include:

items: Yogurt with berries or apple slices
Small sandwiches or bread filled with grated cheese, mashed tuna, salmon, or sardines, served with salad
Salad vegetables such as carrot, celery, or cucumber
Smoothies made with milk, yogurt, and fruit

body.text: Staying hydrated
Water is essential during pregnancy. Adequate hydration supports:
Aim to drink enough water throughout the day, increasing intake during hot weather or exercise.
Foods to limit or avoid
Certain foods carry a higher risk of foodborne illness or excessive exposure to harmful substances.

items: Raw or undercooked meat: there is a small risk of toxoplasmosis from eating raw, undercooked, or cured meat, and this infection can lead to miscarriage. Cold-cured, ready-to-eat meats can also contain Listeria, which may cause listeriosis. Listeriosis can result in miscarriage or stillbirth and can make a newborn baby ill.
Raw fish and raw shellfish; high-mercury fish.
Raw eggs: Salmonella can cause food poisoning, which may make you seriously unwell.

Unpasteurized milk and yogurt, and soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk: unpasteurized dairy products can carry Listeria, a bacterium that causes listeriosis. This infection can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, or severe illness in a newborn baby.
Alcohol: drinking alcohol during pregnancy can cause long-term harm to your baby, so the safest choice is to avoid alcohol entirely.
Excessive caffeine: keep daily caffeine intake below 200 mg, as higher amounts have been linked to an increased risk of miscarriage and stillbirth.

body.text: Wash fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating.
Healthy eating tips
Simple habits can make healthy eating easier:

items: Eat regular meals and avoid long intervals between meals
Fill half your plate with vegetables
Choose whole grains over refined grains
Eat a variety of colourful foods
Take prenatal vitamins as advised by your healthcare provider

body.text: Prepare meals safely

items: Wash fruit, vegetables, and salads thoroughly to remove soil that may contain toxoplasma
Clean hands, surfaces, and utensils before and after preparing raw foods to reduce the risk of food poisoning
Store raw foods separately from ready-to-eat foods to prevent contamination
Use separate knives and chopping boards for raw meat and other foods
Heat ready meals until steaming hot throughout, especially those containing poultry
Check use-by dates and avoid eating food past its use-by date
Ensure foods such as eggs, poultry, burgers, sausages, and whole cuts of lamb or beef are cooked thoroughly until steaming hot all the way through

body.text: Vegetarian or vegan eating patterns during pregnancy

Women who follow vegetarian or vegan eating patterns during pregnancy may need to pay extra attention to meeting their nutrient needs. Iron can be a particular concern because plant foods provide only non-haem iron, which is less readily absorbed than haem iron. Vitamin B12 is another key nutrient, as it is found exclusively in animal-derived foods.

body.title: Discuss supplements with a healthcare provider
body.text: Pregnant women who eat vegetarian or vegan diets should speak with a healthcare provider to determine whether they need supplements such as iron, vitamin B12, or other nutrients including choline, zinc, iodine, or DHA.
When to seek professional advice
Speak with your healthcare provider or a registered dietitian if you:

items: Have severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhoea
Follow a vegetarian or vegan diet

body.text: Individual nutritional needs vary, and personalized advice is often the best approach.
A balanced approach

Healthy eating during pregnancy is not about following a perfect diet—it is about making consistent, nutritious choices that support both you and your baby’s health. A balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, dairy or fortified alternatives, healthy fats, and plenty of water provides most of the nutrients needed for a healthy pregnancy.

Remember that prenatal vitamins complement, but do not replace, a healthy diet. Regular antenatal care, food safety, appropriate supplementation, and guidance from your healthcare provider all play important roles in supporting a healthy pregnancy and giving your baby the best possible start in life.

faq.question: Can I eat eggs during pregnancy?
faq.answer: Yes. Fully cooked eggs are an excellent source of protein, choline, and vitamins. Avoid raw eggs.

faq.question: Is fish safe during pregnancy?
faq.answer: Fish such as salmon, sardines, and trout are safe and provide beneficial omega-3 fatty acids. Limit oily fish such as salmon, trout, mackerel, sardines, and herring.
items: No more than 2 portions of oily fish per week
Avoid high-mercury fish such as shark, swordfish, and marlin

faq.question: How much water should I drink?
faq.answer: Most pregnant women should drink enough fluids to stay well hydrated, though individual needs vary depending on activity level, climate, and medical conditions.

faq.question: Do I need prenatal vitamins if I eat well?
faq.answer: Prenatal vitamins help provide nutrients such as folic acid, iron, and vitamin D that may sometimes be difficult to obtain in sufficient amounts through diet alone.

faq.question: Can I drink coffee?
faq.answer: Moderate caffeine intake is generally considered acceptable during pregnancy, but total caffeine should be limited to less than 200 mg per day, following current recommendations.

faq.question: What foods can help relieve constipation during pregnancy?
faq.answer: High-fibre foods such as whole grains, oats, fresh fruits, vegetables, beans, lentils, and chia seeds can help prevent constipation. Drinking plenty of water and staying physically active, if medically appropriate, can also improve bowel function.
